title: A table, two loops deep

prereqs.why: A loop inside a loop, where the inner one runs from the start again on every pass of the outer one.
Putting a space between numbers but not after the last one is one test inside the inner loop.

statement:
Read one integer `n` and print an `n` by `n` multiplication table.
Row `i` column `j` holds `i * j`, counting both from 1.

```
input:   3

output:  1 2 3
         2 4 6
         3 6 9
```

Numbers in a row are separated by a **single space**, and there is
**no space at the end of a line**. Every row ends with a newline,
including the last.

### The point of the problem

A loop inside a loop. The outer one walks the rows, the inner one
walks the columns of the row it is in, and the inner one runs all
the way through on **every** pass of the outer one:

```
for each row i from 1 to n
    for each column j from 1 to n
        print the entry
    end the line
```

The inner loop runs all the way through on every pass of the outer
one, so its body happens `n * n` times in total. Declare each counter
in its own loop header and the inner one starts again from 1 by
itself.

Where the newline goes is the structural question, and there are
three places it could go. Inside the inner loop it prints one number
per line; after both loops it prints the whole table on one line. Only
one of the three is right, and no compiler will tell you which.

### The separator

"Space between, none at the end" is the standard small nuisance of
printing a list. Printing a space after every number leaves one at the
end of each line, which is a wrong answer you cannot see. The usual
fix is to print the separator **before** every item except the first,
which turns "strip the last one" into a test on the column number.

### Constraints

`n` is between 1 and 12 inclusive, so the largest entry is 144 and
the columns are not expected to line up — single spaces, not padding.

### Boundary cases

- **`n = 1`** is one line containing `1`, with no space anywhere.
- **`n = 2`** is the smallest case where the separator rule is
  visible at all.
- A trailing space on any line is a wrong answer, and is invisible
  when you look at your own output. If a case fails and the line
  looks right, suspect that first.
hints: Two `for` loops, one inside the other. Get the shape right before worrying about spaces: print every number followed by a space, check the rows are correct, and fix the separator afterwards.
The newline belongs to the row, so it goes in the outer loop after the inner loop has finished — not inside the inner loop.
For the separator, print a space *before* each number except the first in its row: `if (j > 1) std::cout << ' ';`. Printing it after each number leaves one at the end of every line.
